chapterTitle: Ch 43. Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image

concepts.title: Depth Estimation as a Regression Problem

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Monocular Depth Cues

concepts.one_liner: Depth estimation can be formulated as a regression problem to recover scene structure from a single image.
concepts.content: We will formulate depth estimation as a regression problem to recover scene structure from a single image.
concepts.motivation_md: Treating depth as a regression problem allows the use of statistical and machine learning tools to predict continuous distance values for every pixel in a 2D image.
concepts.recap_md:
- Depth estimation aims to recover 3D scene structure from a single 2D image.
 - The problem is formulated as a regression task to predict distance values.

concepts.title: Shading as a Monocular Depth Cue

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Monocular Depth Cues

concepts.one_liner: Shading refers to image intensity changes produced by surface orientation variations relative to a light source.
concepts.content: Shading refers to the changes in image intensity produced by changes in surface orientation. The amount of light reflected in the direction of the viewer by a surface illuminated by a directional light source is a function of the surface albedo, the light intensity, and the relative angle between the light direction and the surface normal orientation.
concepts.motivation_md: Shading provides critical information about the 3D shape of objects from a single viewpoint by linking pixel intensity to surface geometry.
concepts.recap_md:
- Shading is caused by variations in surface orientation relative to light.
 - Reflected light depends on albedo, light intensity, and the surface normal angle.

slots.motivation: Shading provides critical information about the 3D shape of objects from a single viewpoint by linking pixel intensity to surface geometry.
slots.key_passage:
- Shading is caused by variations in surface orientation relative to light.
 - Reflected light depends on albedo, light intensity, and the surface normal angle.
slots.example: Shading refers to the changes in image intensity produced by changes in surface orientation. The amount of light reflected in the direction of the viewer by a surface illuminated by a directional light source is a function of the surface albedo, the light intensity, and the relative angle between the light direction and the surface normal orientation.

concepts.title: Shape from Shading

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Monocular Depth Cues

concepts.one_liner: Shape from shading is the study of recovering 3D shape by inverting rendering equations.
concepts.content: Shape from shading studies how to recover shape by inverting the rendering equations.
concepts.motivation_md: By mathematically reversing the process of how light creates shadows and highlights, we can reconstruct the 3D geometry of an object from a single 2D image.
concepts.recap_md:
- Shape from shading aims to recover 3D geometry from intensity variations.
 - It involves inverting the rendering equations that describe light-surface interaction.

concepts.title: Texture Gradients as a Monocular Depth Cue

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Monocular Depth Cues

concepts.one_liner: Texture gradients provide depth information by measuring the relative size of textural elements across different image regions.
concepts.content:
Another source of 3D information are texture gradients. As far things appear smaller than closer things, by measuring the relative size between textural elements that appear in different image regions we can get a coarse estimate of the 3D scene structure (see Figure (a)). Many methods using texture gradient cues have been proposed over time.

concepts.motivation_md: Texture gradients allow the brain and computer vision systems to infer depth and surface orientation based on the systematic shrinking of repeating patterns as they recede.

 - Measuring relative sizes of texture elements provides a coarse 3D scene estimate.

concepts.title: Shadows and Interreflections as Monocular Depth Cues

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Monocular Depth Cues

concepts.one_liner: Shadows and interreflections serve as monocular cues that inform the visual system about the 3D location and structure of objects.
concepts.content: Another source of information about the 3D scene structure are shadows and interreflections. Interreflections can inform us about the location of an object, such as a ball. The use of shadows and interreflections by the human visual system has been the focus of many studies, and there are also computational approaches that use these cues to recover 3D structure.
concepts.motivation_md: Shadows and light bouncing between surfaces provide spatial context, helping to determine the relative distance between objects and their proximity to ground planes.
concepts.recap_md:
- Shadows and interreflections provide cues about object location and 3D structure.
 - These cues are utilized by both the human visual system and computational algorithms.

concepts.title: Aerial Perspective

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Monocular Depth Cues

concepts.one_liner: Aerial perspective is a depth cue where distant objects appear with lower contrast due to atmospheric dispersion.
concepts.content:
When looking at large landscapes, like a mountain range, mountains that are far away have lower contrast due to dispersion by the atmosphere (see [FIGURE:52838648eb2a6dee | ...]). This effect gets accentuated when there is fog. Therefore, contrast can be used as a cue to infer relative distances between objects. This depth cue is called aerial perspective or atmospheric perspective.

[FIGURE:74c32638e485d003 | A close-up photograph of a textured metal surface with a repeating grid of small, square-based pyramidal bumps. The perspective view shows the bumps receding into the distance, illustrating how...]

[FIGURE:52838648eb2a6dee | A photograph of a deep mountain valley illustrating aerial perspective. The foreground mountains are dark green and high contrast, while the distant mountain peaks appear lighter, bluer, and lower in...]

Fig (a) This image contains multiple 3D cues: shading effects (bump shapes), texture gradients (relative size between bumps), and linear perspective (due to the regular arrangement of the bumps). (b) Aerial perspective. Objects far in the background have lower contrast than objects closer to the camera.
concepts.motivation_md: Aerial perspective allows for depth estimation over very long distances where other cues like binocular vision or motion parallax are less effective.
concepts.recap_md:
- Distant objects have lower contrast and often appear bluer due to atmospheric dispersion.
 - Fog or haze accentuates this effect, making it a useful cue for inferring relative distance.

concepts.title: Familiar Objects as Monocular Depth Cues

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Monocular Depth Cues

concepts.one_liner: Depth can be estimated by detecting familiar objects with known sizes to determine absolute distance.
concepts.content: Depth can be estimated by detecting familiar objects with known sizes. One example is people detection. Objects with known sizes can be used to estimate absolute depth, while many other cues can only provide relative depth measurements. One example of using object sizes to reason about 3D geometry is found in @Hoiem2008.
concepts.motivation_md: While many monocular cues only provide relative depth (which object is closer), knowing the physical size of a familiar object allows a system to calculate the absolute distance from the camera.

concepts.title: 3D Representations

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: 3D Representations

concepts.one_liner: 3D information can be represented in various formats, including disparity maps, depth maps, point clouds, and meshes.
concepts.content: 3D information can be represented in many different ways, such as disparity maps, depth maps, planes, 3D point clouds, voxels, implicit functions, surface normals, and meshes. There are specific methods tailored for each of these representations. In this context, we primarily focus on depth maps or disparity maps, where disparity is related to the inverse of depth.
concepts.motivation_md: Different applications in computer vision and graphics require different data structures; for example, depth maps are convenient for sensors, while meshes are preferred for rendering surfaces.

concepts.title: Translating Depth Maps to 3D Point Clouds

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: 3D Representations

concepts.one_liner: Translating a depth map into a 3D point cloud requires mapping each pixel to a 3D point using intrinsic camera parameters.
concepts.content:
Translating a depth map into a point cloud requires a calibrated camera with known intrinsic parameters. Each pixel $(n,m)$ is mapped into a 3D point, $\mathbf{P}$, by using the depth, $z[n,m]$, at that location.

Using homogeneous coordinates, the equation translating a depth map into a 3D point cloud for each pixel is:
$$\mathbf{P} = z(\mathbf{p}) \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{p}$$
where $\mathbf{p}$ are the pixel coordinates, $z(\mathbf{p})$ is the depth measured at that location, and $\mathbf{P}$ are the final 3D point coordinates. In heterogeneous coordinates, making the pixel locations explicit, the equation can be rewritten as:
$$\begin{aligned}
    X[n,m] &= \left( n-c_x \right) \frac{z[n,m]}{a} \\
    Y[n,m] &= \left( m-c_y \right) \frac{z[n,m]}{a} \\
    Z[n,m] &= z[n,m] 
\end{aligned}$$
where $a$, $c_x$ and $c_y$ are the intrinsic camera parameters in pixel units. This shows that the 3D point coordinates are represented by three images $X[n,m]$, $Y[n,m]$, and $Z[n,m]$ of the same size as the input image.
concepts.motivation_md: To perform 3D reasoning or navigation, we must convert 2D image-plane depth measurements into a standard 3D coordinate system (X, Y, Z).
concepts.recap_md: [ - The transformation uses the inverse of the intrinsic matrix $\mathbf{K}$ and the depth value $z$. ]

slots.motivation: To perform 3D reasoning or navigation, we must convert 2D image-plane depth measurements into a standard 3D coordinate system (X, Y, Z).
slots.key_passage: [ - The transformation uses the inverse of the intrinsic matrix $\mathbf{K}$ and the depth value $z$. ]

concepts.title: Turbo and Jet Colormaps for Depth Visualization

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: 3D Representations

concepts.one_liner: The turbo colormap is a modified version of the jet colormap used to visualize depth maps and distinguish them from grayscale images.
concepts.content:
Depth maps are usually visualized using the **turbo colormap**, which is a modification of the **jet colormap** from Matlab. We use this convention to differentiate a depth map from a natural gray-scale image.

[FIGURE:5e64d445bf392d94 | Two vertical color bars labeled 'Jet' and 'Turbo' showing rainbow color maps used for depth visualization. Both bars transition from dark blue at the bottom, labeled 'Near', through cyan, green...]

The jet colormap can be problematic as it has a nonmonotonic intensity profile.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard grayscale images represent intensity, while depth maps represent distance; using a specific colormap like Turbo helps humans visually interpret depth gradients more clearly.

concepts.title: Point Clouds vs. Meshes

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Supervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Point clouds consist of isolated 3D points, while meshes connect points into surfaces using triangles.
concepts.content: In a point cloud, there is no notion of grouping of 3D points; points are isolated and not connected to each other. Translating a depth map or a point cloud into a mesh requires solving the perceptual organization problem first. A mesh connects points with triangles, but it only makes sense to connect points that belong to the same surface or that are in contact.
concepts.motivation_md: Point clouds are the direct output of many sensors, but meshes are necessary for defining continuous surfaces and volumes in graphics and simulation.

concepts.title: Supervised Depth Estimation Formulation

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Supervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Supervised depth estimation is formulated as a pixelwise regression problem where a model learns to predict depth maps from images.
concepts.content:
In the supervised setting, we assume a training set containing $N$ images, $\ell^{(i)} [n,m]$, and their associated depth maps, $z^{(i)} [n,m]$. Depth estimation is formulated as a pixelwise regression problem. Typically, $\mathbf{z}^{(i)}$ and $\boldsymbol\ell^{(i)}$ are images of the same size. The goal is to estimate depth at each pixel, $\hat{z}^{(i)}[n,m]$, from a single image using a learnable function $h_\theta$:
$$\hat{\mathbf{z}}^{(i)} = h_\theta \left( \boldsymbol\ell^{(i)} \right)$$
The parameters $\theta$ are learned by minimizing the loss over the training set:
$$\theta^* = \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{\theta} \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \mathcal{L} \left( \hat{\mathbf{z}}^{(i)}, \mathbf{z}^{(i)} \right)$$
concepts.motivation_md: By treating depth estimation as a supervised regression task, we can leverage deep learning to predict 3D structure from 2D images using ground-truth data.
concepts.recap_md: [ - Supervised depth estimation uses a learnable function to map images to depth maps. ]

slots.motivation: By treating depth estimation as a supervised regression task, we can leverage deep learning to predict 3D structure from 2D images using ground-truth data.
slots.key_passage: [ - Supervised depth estimation uses a learnable function to map images to depth maps. ]

concepts.title: LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging)

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Supervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: LiDAR is a device that calculates distances by measuring the time taken for emitted light to return after reflecting off a surface.
concepts.content: LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) is a device that calculates distances by measuring the time taken for emitted light to return after reflecting off a surface (time of flight). A LiDAR produces a range image by scanning multiple directions. The output of this process is a point cloud. It is a common data capture method for depth sensing, alongside other sensors such as RGB-D cameras.
concepts.motivation_md: LiDAR provides a direct way to measure 3D geometry by using light pulses, solving the problem of estimating distance from 2D images alone.
concepts.recap_md:
- Measures distance using the time of flight of emitted light.
 - Scans multiple directions to produce a range image.
 - Generates a point cloud as its primary output.

concepts.title: Data Collection for Supervised Depth Estimation

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Supervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Supervised depth estimation relies on datasets captured via sensors like Kinect and LiDAR, or reconstructed through multiview geometry and stereo pairs.
concepts.content: Datasets for supervised depth estimation are collected using various methods. Examples include the NYUv2 dataset, captured using a handheld Microsoft Kinect sensor in indoor environments, and the KITTI dataset, collected from a moving vehicle equipped with a LiDAR scan. Other methods utilize stereo pairs for training or multiview geometry techniques to provide accurate 3D estimates. For instance, MegaDepth uses scenes captured with multiple cameras to generate 3D reconstructions via structure from motion, creating datasets of images and associated depth maps for training single-image depth estimation models.
concepts.motivation_md: To train neural networks for depth estimation, large-scale ground truth data is required to teach the model the relationship between 2D pixels and 3D distance.
concepts.recap_md:
- Sensors like Kinect (RGB-D) and LiDAR provide direct ground truth depth maps.
 - Structure from motion and multiview geometry can generate depth data from multiple images.
 - Stereo pairs are also used as a source of training data for depth estimation.

 - Stereo pairs are also used as a source of training data for depth estimation.

concepts.title: L2 Loss for Depth Estimation

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Supervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: The L2 loss for depth estimation calculates the sum of squared differences between estimated and ground truth depth values.
concepts.content:
One simple loss used to optimize the parameters of a depth estimator is the L2 loss. This loss measures the difference between the estimated depth, $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$, and the ground truth depth, $\mathbf{z}$:

$$\mathcal{L} \left( \hat{\mathbf{z}}, \mathbf{z} \right) =  \sum_{n,m} \left( \hat{z}[n,m] - z[n,m] \right) ^2$$
concepts.motivation_md: The L2 loss provides a straightforward mathematical objective to minimize the distance between predicted and actual depth values during training.
concepts.recap_md:
- Computes the squared difference between predicted and actual depth at each pixel.
 - Sums these differences across all pixels $(n, m)$ in the image.
 - Serves as a basic optimization target for depth estimation parameters.

 - Sums these differences across all pixels $(n, m)$ in the image.
 - Serves as a basic optimization target for depth estimation parameters.

concepts.title: Scale-Invariant Loss

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Supervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: The scale-invariant loss addresses global scale factors by eliminating the average difference between estimated and ground truth depth.
concepts.content:
The scale-invariant loss addresses the issue of global scale factors by eliminating the global scale factor from the calculation:
$$\mathcal{L} \left( \hat{\mathbf{z}}, \mathbf{z} \right) =  \sum_{n,m} \left( \hat{z}[n,m] - z[n,m] - \alpha\right) ^2$$
where $\alpha = \frac{1}{NM} \sum_{n,m} \hat{z}[n,m] - z[n,m]$. This loss compares the estimated and ground truth depth at each pixel while accounting for a constant offset.
concepts.motivation_md: In many depth estimation tasks, the relative depth is more important than the absolute scale, which might be unknown or inconsistent across datasets.
concepts.recap_md:
- Eliminates global scale factors using a calculated offset $\alpha$.
 - $\alpha$ represents the mean difference between estimated and ground truth depth.
 - Focuses on the relative depth structure rather than absolute distance values.

concepts.title: Log-Depth and Disparity Optimization

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Supervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Optimizing for log-depth or disparity helps mitigate large errors associated with distant points in depth estimation.
concepts.content: Standard depth estimation can result in large errors for points with large depth values. One way to mitigate this is to optimize the reconstruction of the log of the depth, $\log \left( z[n,m] \right)$, or the disparity, which corresponds to the inverse of the depth, $1/z[n,m]$.
concepts.motivation_md: Linear depth scales penalize errors at long distances too heavily; log-depth and disparity provide a more balanced error distribution.
concepts.recap_md:
- Log-depth optimization uses $\log(z)$ to handle large depth ranges.
 - Disparity optimization uses $1/z$, the inverse of depth.
 - These methods reduce the impact of high-magnitude errors at large distances.

concepts.title: Encoder-Decoder Architecture for Depth Estimation

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Supervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Depth estimation is typically implemented using an encoder-decoder neural network with skip connections to map RGB images to depth maps.
concepts.content:
The depth estimation function is usually implemented with a neural network using an encoder-decoder architecture with skip connections. The input is a red-green-blue (RGB) image and the output is a depth map. While this architecture is generic and not specific to depth estimation, one could add constraints such as a preference for planar shapes or other structural priors. However, most current approaches use a fairly generic architecture and let the data and the loss function determine the best mapping.

(see figure: Typical architecture for depth estimation from a single image @Xian2018)
concepts.motivation_md: Encoder-decoder structures are effective at capturing global context while preserving local spatial details necessary for accurate per-pixel depth prediction.
concepts.recap_md:
- Uses an encoder-decoder structure to transform RGB inputs into depth maps.
 - Skip connections help preserve spatial detail from the input image.
 - Often relies on data-driven learning rather than hard-coded structural priors.

concepts.title: Visualizing 3D Reconstruction Quality

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Supervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: The best way to evaluate a 3D reconstruction is to translate the depth map into a point cloud and view it from different perspectives.
concepts.content:
Just looking at a 2D depth map might make estimates appear good, but it is hard to tell the true quality of the estimation with that visualization. The best way of appreciating the quality of a 3D reconstruction is by translating the depth map into a point cloud and then reconstructing the scene under different view points. Points near regions of depth discontinuities are often removed to improve the clarity of the visualization, as these points are frequently incorrect and tend to have depth values that are the average of the values on each side of the discontinuity.

[FIGURE:349fd762fb7f8019 | A 3D point cloud reconstruction of an office scene viewed from a perspective angle. The image shows a bookshelf filled with books on the left, a small round wooden table in the foreground, and a desk...]

[FIGURE:ab4a3ae0938f2ef6 | A 3D point cloud reconstruction of an office scene, viewed from a high-angle perspective. The reconstruction shows a blue carpeted floor, some furniture elements like a wooden table or desk, and wall...]

Reconstructed point cloud of the office scene with two different view points. Results are good, but not great.
concepts.motivation_md: 2D depth maps can hide errors in geometry; 3D point cloud visualization reveals artifacts and inaccuracies in the reconstructed spatial structure.

- Depth maps are converted to point clouds for better quality assessment.
 - Viewing the reconstruction from multiple angles reveals geometric errors.
 - Depth discontinuities are often filtered out because they contain averaged, inaccurate values.

concepts.title: Scale Calibration from Known Distances

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Supervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: If we are given one real distance, we can calibrate a 3D reconstruction that otherwise has an arbitrary scaling.
concepts.content: The point cloud has an arbitrary scaling, so we cannot directly use it to make 3D measurements. However, if we are given one real distance, we can calibrate the 3D reconstruction.
concepts.motivation_md: 3D reconstructions from point clouds often lack absolute scale, meaning we know the relative positions but not the actual size. Providing a single known distance allows us to map the arbitrary units to real-world measurements.
concepts.recap_md: - Point clouds generated from images typically have an arbitrary scale.

concepts.title: Unsupervised Depth from a Single Image

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Unsupervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Unsupervised methods learn to perceive depth from single images by using motion and temporal consistency as a supervisory signal instead of ground truth data.
concepts.content: Although supervised techniques can be very effective, unsupervised techniques are more likely to eventually reach higher accuracy as they can learn from much larger amounts of data and improve over time. Unsupervised techniques pose a grander intellectual challenge: How can a system learn to perceive depth from a camera without supervision? We assume that the camera is calibrated, meaning the intrinsic camera parameters are known. There are a number of approaches one could imagine; for instance, we could use some of the single view metrology techniques to generate supervisory data. A different, and likely simpler, approach would be to use motion and temporal consistency as a supervisory signal.
concepts.motivation_md: Supervised depth estimation requires massive amounts of ground truth data, which is hard to collect. Unsupervised methods solve this by using the inherent geometric consistency of video sequences as a self-supervisory signal.
concepts.recap_md: - Unsupervised depth estimation leverages large datasets without needing manual ground truth labels.

slots.motivation: Supervised depth estimation requires massive amounts of ground truth data, which is hard to collect. Unsupervised methods solve this by using the inherent geometric consistency of video sequences as a self-supervisory signal.
slots.key_passage: - Unsupervised depth estimation leverages large datasets without needing manual ground truth labels.

concepts.title: Image Prediction Formulation for Unsupervised Depth

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Unsupervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Unsupervised depth learning can be formulated as an image prediction problem where pixel values between frames are related by scene structure and camera motion.
concepts.content: As a camera moves in the world, the pixel values between two images captured at two different time instants are related by the 3D scene structure and the relative camera motion between the two frames. Therefore, we can formulate the problem as an image prediction problem. Let's say we have a function $f_1$ that can estimate depth from a single image, and a function $f_2$ that takes as input two frames, $\boldsymbol\ell_1$ and $\boldsymbol\ell_2$, and estimates the relative camera positions (the rotation and translation matrices, $\mathbf{R}$ and $\mathbf{T}$) between the two frames, as shown in (see figure: System for unsupervised learning of camera motion and depth @Tinghui2017. The goal is to learn the parameters of the functions $f_1$ and $f_2$ by minimizing the reconstruction error. The function...): $$\begin{aligned} \hat{\mathbf{z}} &= f_1(\boldsymbol\ell) \\ \left[ \hat{\mathbf{R}},\hat{\mathbf{T}} \right] &= f_2(\boldsymbol\ell_1,\boldsymbol\ell_2) \end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: By framing depth estimation as an image prediction task, we can use the difference between a predicted frame and an actual frame as a loss function, removing the need for explicit depth labels.
concepts.recap_md: - The system uses one function to estimate depth and another to estimate relative camera motion.

The function...): $$\begin{aligned} \hat{\mathbf{z}} &= f_1(\boldsymbol\ell) \\ \left[ \hat{\mathbf{R}},\hat{\mathbf{T}} \right] &= f_2(\boldsymbol\ell_1,\boldsymbol\ell_2) \end{aligned}$$

concepts.title: Backward Warping for Unsupervised Depth Supervision

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Unsupervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Backward warping uses estimated depth and camera motion to map pixels from a reference frame to a target frame, providing a geometric constraint for unsupervised learning.
concepts.content: If the estimations of the depth and camera motion were correct, then we could warp the pixels in $\boldsymbol\ell_1$ into the pixels of $\boldsymbol\ell_2$ as depth and camera motion is all we need to precisely predict how the corresponding 3D points will move between the two frames. Warping is a deterministic function ($f_3$ in @fig-unsupervised_depth_system) that takes as input a reference frame, the depth map, and the relative camera motion matrices and outputs an image: $$\boldsymbol\ell_{1 \rightarrow 2} = f_3(\boldsymbol\ell_1, \mathbf{z}, \mathbf{R}, \mathbf{T})$$ The goal is to warp a reference frame into a target frame. For each pixel location $\mathbf{x}$ in the target frame $\boldsymbol\ell_2$, we compute the corresponding location on the reference frame $\boldsymbol\ell_1$ using these steps: 1. Express the image coordinates of the pixel in the target frame in homogeneous coordinates, $\mathbf{p}$. 2. Recover the 3D world coordinates of the target point, $\mathbf{P}$, using the known intrinsic camera matrix and the estimated depth: $\mathbf{P} = z(\mathbf{p}) \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{p}$, where $\hat{\mathbf{z}} = f_1(\boldsymbol\ell_2)$. 3. Use the camera rotation and translation matrices to change the camera coordinates to those of the reference frame: $\mathbf{P}' = \mathbf{M}\mathbf{P}$. 4. Project the point $\mathbf{P}'$ into the image coordinates of the reference frame: $\mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{K} \mathbf{P}'$. 5. Translate the resulting coordinates $\mathbf{p}'$ back into heterogeneous coordinates. (see figure: Geometry between two images captured by a moving camera. The coordinates of corresponding points between the two frames are constrained by the 3D world coordinates of the point the relative camera...)
concepts.motivation_md: Backward warping allows us to synthesize a target image from a reference image using predicted geometry. The difference between this synthesized image and the real target image acts as the training signal.
concepts.recap_md: - Backward warping maps target frame pixels back to a reference frame using estimated depth and motion.

concepts.title: Unsupervised Depth Reconstruction Loss

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Unsupervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: The unsupervised depth loss measures the pixel-wise difference between a target image and a reconstruction generated by warping a reference image.
concepts.content: Putting all these steps together, ignoring the transformations between homogeneous and heterogeneous coordinates, the reconstruction of $\boldsymbol\ell_2$ results in: $$\ell_{1 \rightarrow 2}(\mathbf{p}) = \ell_1 \left( \mathbf{K} \hat{\mathbf{M}} \hat{z}(\mathbf{p}) \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{p} \right)$$ where $\boldsymbol\ell_{1 \rightarrow 2}$ is the result of warping image $\boldsymbol\ell_1$ into $\boldsymbol\ell_2$. As the coordinates of the point $\mathbf{p}'$ will not be discrete, we use bilinear interpolation to estimate the pixel value. If the reconstruction is correct, we expect the difference $\left| \ell_{1 \rightarrow 2}(\mathbf{p}) - \ell_{2}(\mathbf{p}) \right|$ to be very small. The functions $f_1$ and $f_2$ can be neural networks and their parameters can be obtained by running back-propagation over the loss: $$\mathcal{L} = \sum_{n,m} v\left(n,m \right) \left( \ell_{1 \rightarrow 2}[n,m] - \ell_{2}[n,m] \right) ^2$$
concepts.motivation_md: To train a model without ground truth depth, we need a proxy loss. The photometric error between the warped reference frame and the actual target frame serves as this proxy.
concepts.recap_md: - The loss function calculates the squared difference between the warped reference image and the target image.

concepts.title: Valid Pixel Masking in Depth Learning

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Unsupervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Valid pixel masking restricts the depth learning loss to pixels that are visible in both frames and not part of moving objects.
concepts.content: As only the pixels with coordinates $\mathbf{p}'$ inside the image can be reconstructed by warping, we compute the loss only over the valid set of pixels. This is done using the mask $v\left(n,m \right)$, which is 1 for valid pixels and 0 for pixels that lie outside the visible part of the reference frame. The mask could also exclude pixels that fall in moving objects as those will have displacements that cannot predicted by the motion of the camera alone.
concepts.motivation_md: Not all pixels in a target frame can be found in a reference frame due to camera motion or occlusions. Masking prevents the model from being penalized for errors it cannot geometrically resolve.
concepts.recap_md: - A binary mask $v(n,m)$ identifies which pixels should contribute to the reconstruction loss.

slots.motivation: Not all pixels in a target frame can be found in a reference frame due to camera motion or occlusions. Masking prevents the model from being penalized for errors it cannot geometrically resolve.

concepts.title: Camera Motion Requirements for Depth Learning

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Unsupervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Learning depth from single images requires complex camera motions in rich 3D environments to distinguish depth from simple image transformations.
concepts.content: Not all camera motions provide enough information to learn about the 3D world structure. As discussed in the context of homographies, if all the videos contain only sequences captured by a rotating camera, the points are related by a homography regardless of the 3D structure. Therefore, to learn depth from single images, we need to have complex camera motions inside environments with rich 3D structure.
concepts.motivation_md: Pure rotation doesn't produce parallax, which is the primary cue for depth. Without translation, a system cannot distinguish between a flat image and a 3D scene.
concepts.recap_md: - Purely rotating cameras produce homographies that do not reveal 3D scene structure.

slots.motivation: Pure rotation doesn't produce parallax, which is the primary cue for depth. Without translation, a system cannot distinguish between a flat image and a 3D scene.
slots.key_passage: - Purely rotating cameras produce homographies that do not reveal 3D scene structure.

The idea of learning depth from single images is constrained by the types of camera motion present in the training data.

overlay.rationale: Unsupervised techniques are contrasted with supervised methods, which require ground truth data but may eventually be surpassed by unsupervised methods learning from larger datasets.
